inline.s: Q: I have recited the Buddha's name for many years and have formed the habit of silently reciting it in my mind while walking. Now that I am practicing awareness of movements, may I still silently recite the Buddha's name while walking?

A: Yes. But while reciting, you should be focusedly aware of the movements and feelings of your feet. You will come to experience that reciting as you walk leaves you with few wandering thoughts, or none at all. When your awareness is powerful, you will also be clearly aware of the very thought of reciting, and you will see wandering thoughts as they arise. At that point, reciting the Buddha's name approaches one mind undisturbed.
Q: Keeping awareness going without a break sounds easy — one need only not forget — but I find it extremely difficult in practice. Where does the problem lie?

A: The problem lies in habit and in karmic hindrance. As for habit, it is enough to do away with the old habit of carelessness and cultivate the new habit of clear and distinct knowing. If, however, the obstruction comes from karmic hindrance, then you must examine whether you strictly observe the five precepts and the ten wholesome deeds, and you must repent and purify your karmic hindrance. Reciting the Sutra of the Past Vows of Earth Store Bodhisattva once each day and dedicating the merit is extremely effective for eradicating karmic hindrance.

There is another effective method for keeping awareness going without a break. For one who recites the Buddha's name, the basic requirement is that the recitation never be interrupted — as it is said, "Before attaining one mind undisturbed, first make it unbroken." First require of yourself that the Buddha's name be unbroken, that is, that you recite at all times and in all places. On that basis, with each recitation be aware of the movement of the present moment; if there is no movement, be aware of whatever is present before you — a cup, a table, and so on.

If your awareness is focused and continuous, you will discover something wonderful: ordinarily, reciting the Buddha's name is always mixed with wandering thoughts, but when you recite one recitation and at the same time are aware of movement, no wandering thoughts arise. Especially when you have practiced the method of "recite and immediately be aware" rather deeply, so that awareness is focused and continuous
(wandering thoughts arise precisely in the gaps where awareness is not continuous)
, it becomes very easy to recite the Buddha's name free of wandering thoughts.

Feelings may be mental or physical, and the two are often closely linked. Emotions — contentment, happiness, craving, envy, discontent, pain, resentment, blame, sorrow, depression, emptiness, fear, anxiety, anger, and so on — all give rise to feelings of body and mind.

To be aware of feelings, and to be aware whether one is clinging to them (taking them as real), and thereby to realize their illusory and impermanent nature so as not to be controlled by them — this is cultivation; and further
one arrives at the state where there is only awareness and only contemplation,
beyond clinging, no longer grasping at anything in body, mind, or world"
(The Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness). 1

To be aware of feelings is to observe and know them objectively (in the role of an observer) and without judgment. Through awareness of feelings one can know the mind more precisely and can calm emotions and wandering thoughts; one should be perfectly clear about one's feelings in the present moment.

To be aware of feelings of body and mind without judgment not only releases negative emotions so that one is neither harmed nor controlled by them, but is also the perfect opportunity to uproot the seeds of karma.

Therefore, whenever a negative emotion arises, immediately be aware of and observe, without judgment, the feelings of body and mind it brings about. The more you practice this, the more promptly you will catch negative emotions without being harmed by them, and the more they will become aids on the path to bodhi.
When you are angry (or sad), if you can observe it without judgment in the role of an observer, then although the anger (or sadness) has not subsided, it can no longer control you.

Besides promptly being aware of the feelings aroused by emotions and thereby escaping their control, in the course of daily life we can also cut off wandering thoughts and cultivate awareness by being aware of the feelings aroused by movements. For example: the feeling of the body touching the bed as you sleep; the feeling of the body touching the chair as you sit; the feeling of contact with towel and water as you wash your face; the feeling of contact with the toothbrush as you brush your teeth; the feelings of contact of every kind as you eat, as you wash dishes, as you walk. The benefits of doing this are: first, no wandering thoughts; second, cultivation of awareness. If, while being aware of feelings, you are at the same time aware of the movements that arouse them, this is wonderful and interesting, and the effect is even better — this is cultivation. Extending this further, in the course of a single day you have countless such opportunities for cultivation.

Through unremitting training, once you have mastered the techniques of awareness of movements and awareness of feelings, then, as the Chan patriarchs said, putting on clothes and eating, carrying firewood and drawing water — none of it is other than cultivation. This is the key to making cultivation part of daily life.
In
The Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness
, the World-Honored One taught:

Monks, how does a monk contemplate feelings in feelings? Monks, when experiencing a pleasant feeling, he clearly knows: "I am experiencing a pleasant feeling." When experiencing a painful feeling, he clearly knows: "I am experiencing a painful feeling." When experiencing a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant, he clearly knows: "I am experiencing a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant." When he clings to a pleasant feeling, he clearly knows: "I am clinging to a pleasant feeling." When he does not cling to a pleasant feeling, he clearly knows: "I am not clinging to a pleasant feeling." When he clings to a painful feeling, he clearly knows: "I am clinging to a painful feeling." When he does not cling to a painful feeling, he clearly knows: "I am not clinging to a painful feeling." When he clings to a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant, he clearly knows: "I am clinging to a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant." When he does not cling to a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant, he clearly knows: "I am not clinging to a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant."

Thus he contemplates feelings in feelings internally, he contemplates feelings in feelings externally, and he contemplates feelings in feelings both internally and externally. He contemplates the phenomena that keep arising in feelings, he contemplates the phenomena that keep passing away in feelings, and he contemplates both the arising and the passing away of the phenomena in feelings. He then clearly knows: "This is feeling!"
He arrives at the state where there is only awareness and only contemplation,
beyond clinging, no longer grasping at anything in body, mind, or world. Monks, this is how a monk contemplates feelings in feelings.
Q: I am often shrouded in negative emotions. What should I do?

A: Negative emotions are great enemies of body and mind: they not only make us suffer needless pain but also cause many illnesses. Looking back over your own experience of life, you will find one fact: when you are shrouded in negative emotions, everything, everywhere, goes wrong; conversely, when your heart is kind and your mind joyful, everything, everywhere, goes well. It is therefore very important to detect negative emotions in time and promptly release and dissolve them.
Q: How can one release and dissolve negative emotions?

A: Observe it without judgment, be aware of the feelings it arouses, and watch it with keen interest until this crying, fretful child breaks into a smile. Note that you must have a certain degree of awareness before you can effectively put the above method into practice. If you meet with difficulty in doing so, then, as the preceding chapter on "awareness of movements" explains, further cultivate awareness through awareness of movements.
Q: How can one relieve tension and stress?

A: Look inward: from where do tension and stress arise? Keep looking, and you will enter a state free of tension and stress. Then simply abide in that state free of tension and stress. Relieve tension and stress in this way often, and they will not settle down and run amok.

blocks.text: Chapter Three: Awareness of the Breath

inline.s: Awareness of the breath is built upon the preceding "awareness of movements" and "awareness of feelings." The more solid your foundation in the earlier practices, the more easily this stage will come to hand. If awareness of the breath proves very difficult, you should return to the earlier stages of practice, and only when your awareness is sufficient should you begin to practice awareness of the breath. Each later stage likewise rests upon the stage before it, and so advancing only after each hollow is filled is the best and fastest way.

[Advancing only after each hollow is filled] When spring water meets a hollow, it must fill it before it flows on. This is a metaphor for learning: one should lay a solid foundation and take each step steadily, not rushing ahead impatiently.

Awareness of the breath is subtler than awareness of movements, and since the breath is always present, being aware of it at any time is highly effective for strengthening awareness and greatly beneficial to body and mind.

Because aims differ, there are many ways of contemplating the breath. The awareness of the breath in this chapter serves reciting the Buddha's name to one mind undisturbed, and so it differs from other contemplations. Three methods are introduced below. All are practiced in a still posture; the eyes may be open or closed, and no posture is prescribed — sitting, lying down, or standing are all acceptable; both the in-breath and the out-breath are through the nostrils. Choose one of the three to practice; there is no need to practice them all.

The first method is awareness of the breath at the tip of the nose (abbreviated as contemplating the breath): breathe naturally. In being aware, there is no need to distinguish the in-breath from the out-breath, long from short, heavy from light, slow from fast, and so on; simply know that you are aware of the breath at the tip of the nose, and keep this state continuously, with the body relaxed. The key is: the eyes contemplate the nose. "The eyes contemplate the nose" means drawing the light of the spirit inward from the eyes and shining it back upon the breath at the tip of the nose. (Note: never mistake "the eyes contemplate the nose" for looking at the tip of your nose with your eyes.) When the practice of contemplating the breath is deep, the light of the spirit will come to rest at the tip of the nose, and you will be aware of the breath there at all times.

The second method is the method of contemplating the breath and counting the breath: touch the tongue to the upper palate and breathe from the abdomen — inhale deeply (in-breath), and the abdomen gradually bulges outward; exhale slowly (out-breath), and the abdomen gradually draws inward, and so on in cycles. Take special note: the breathing must be purely natural; do not use force. In time, as the practice deepens, the breath will gradually become fine, deep, long, and slow. Before practicing, first relax body and mind, be serene and at ease, and even out the breath; then you may begin. On the out-breath, silently count six numbers: one, two, three, four, five, six. (Please note that this differs from the traditional method of counting the breath. In the traditional method, you count one on the first out-breath, two on the second out-breath, and so on; in this method, you count six numbers on every out-breath: one, two, three, four, five, six.) On the in-breath, be aware of the inhalation; on the out-breath, be aware of each number you count, with no stray thoughts. If stray thoughts arise, it means that awareness has scattered or been lost altogether; at once rouse yourself with a keen wakefulness and, gathering your spirits, begin again. When the practice of counting the breath is deeper, body and mind become still and collected, and the mind no longer takes pleasure in counting; then stop counting and focus on being aware of the in-breath and out-breath (contemplating the breath). In practice, if states or visions appear — whether good or bad, fair or foul — know that "all that has marks is delusive," neither grasp nor reject them, neither rejoice nor grieve, and focus on being aware of the counting and aware of the breath; then you will not be harmed by them.

The third method is awareness of the rising and falling of the abdomen: breathe from the abdomen. On the in-breath the abdomen bulges outward; on the out-breath it draws inward; the breathing should be natural. When you first begin to practice, you may place your hand on the abdomen and feel its rising and falling. When the practice matures and the mind gradually gathers, you can then take your hand away and still be well aware of the rising and falling of the abdomen.
In addition, when studying and practicing awareness of the breath,
Practical Insight Meditation

is a book whose method is worth learning from; it cultivates awareness by making awareness of the rising and falling of the abdomen its core. Since this borrows the basic exercise section of insight (vipassanā) meditation in order to train and cultivate focused, continuous, and lasting awareness, when using insight meditation books the emphasis should be on reading the basic exercise section.

Awareness of the breath is a most important basic skill. Its functions are: first, to cultivate focused, continuous, and lasting awareness; second, to forge the mind, settling the scattered mind into stillness. The mind is like a wild elephant — frenzied, restless, and enormously destructive — and so it must be tamed before it can be turned from harm to benefit and made to work for us. Awareness of the breath is the taming of the mind; its wonders are hard to put into words. Only keep practicing, and when your skill is a little deeper you will realize for yourself that this is a wonderful method for stilling the mind and putting an end to wandering thoughts; that is why the ancients likened it to a sword that cuts down demons.

Awareness of the breath looks easy but is in fact quite difficult, because attention is at every moment being drawn away by wandering thoughts. The remedy, therefore, is: lose it and recover it at once. That is, as soon as you notice that you have forgotten to be aware of the breath, immediately draw the mind back and be aware of the breath with focus. Once the practice comes to hand, so long as you are aware of the breath there are no wandering thoughts. When your practice is deeper still, then even as wandering thoughts fly up in profusion, so long as you focus on being aware of the breath the wandering thoughts cease — this is the origin of the great name "the sword that cuts down demons." Hence it is said: when wandering thoughts rise in swarms, make contemplation of the breath your anchor.
[Lose it and recover it at once] The moment the mind strays, immediately (that is, at once) bring it back.

The path of practice is this: discover, test, and sum up for yourself a set of methods that will let awareness of the breath stand firm, stand long, and resist distraction. Often ask yourself: Why did I forget to be aware of the breath? What plunged me into this bout of wandering thoughts? As the saying goes, effort never betrays a willing heart. So long as you are sincere, resolute, and able to endure hardship, and you keep practicing, the method will come of itself.

In this stage of practice, sit in awareness of the breath for at least two hours each day. As for the sitting posture, the full lotus, half lotus, or cross-legged posture (legs crossed) are all acceptable, and you may also sit upright on a chair or stool; the best posture is one in which the back is straight (but the chest is not thrust out, and the back does not lean against the chair) and which you can hold steadily and for a long time. In the later stages of "awareness of thoughts" and "awareness while reciting the Buddha's name," the sitting practice must likewise be maintained at least two hours a day, and the more the better.

This practice of awareness of the breath should be done not only while sitting but also a great deal off the cushion: practice while standing (or standing still), while sitting, and while lying down (during walking and movement, practice awareness of movements); practice with the eyes open and with them closed; practice at every available moment — practice! practice! practice!
Q: Some material on abdominal breathing says to hold the breath for one second after inhaling, and also for one second after exhaling. May one use this method?
A: Yes, but do not lose your awareness.
It should be especially pointed out that:
"Feeling the whole body, I breathe in; feeling the whole body, I breathe out." —
This is a most simple, direct, and effective method of cultivation. The World-Honored One taught in The Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness:

"He trains himself thus: 'I shall breathe in feeling the whole body'; he trains himself thus: 'I shall breathe out feeling the whole body.' ... He arrives at the state where there is only awareness and contemplation, beyond clinging, no longer craving anything in body, mind, or world."
(See in detail
The Commentary on the Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness
[Beyond clinging] No habitual reaction arises.

blocks.text: Chapter Four: Awareness of the Present Moment

inline.s: The present moment is this time, this place.
Presence — total presence, at one with the present moment.
Not thinking of the past, not thinking of the future, living in the present moment.
Lose the present moment, and the quality of your life drops greatly.

To be aware of the present moment is to be aware of this time and this place. (This place is wherever the eyes and ears reach.) The key is: toward everything around you, seeing is just seeing, hearing is just hearing, knowing is just knowing, perceiving is just perceiving — without giving rise to thoughts.

There was a practitioner named Bāhiya who, after a long and dusty journey, hurried to Sāvatthī to seek the Dharma from the Buddha. He saw the Buddha walking from house to house in the city on almsround, every gesture and movement graceful and lovely, all six senses governed and guarded, serene and at peace. Bāhiya approached, bowed in homage, and begged the Buddha to teach him the Dharma, to speak to him the Dharma of endless benefit and happiness. The Buddha said that he was now going from door to door on almsround and that it was not a suitable time to teach. But Bāhiya asked again and again, and so the Buddha taught him right where he stood:

"Bāhiya, you should train yourself thus: in the seen there will be only the seen; in the heard, only the heard; in the known, only the known; in the perceived, only the perceived. Bāhiya, when you can manage that — in the seen only the seen, in the heard only the heard, in the known only the known, in the perceived only the perceived — then you will have no clinging or hindrance. Having no clinging or hindrance, you will have no past life and no future life
. With no past and no future, these two lives
(and only the present moment)
, all sorrow, lamentation, pain, and grief are utterly dispelled."
(The original text is found in the Theravāda Udāna.)

[The three periods] The past, present, and future lives. Any dharma that has arisen and ceased is called the "past life"; any dharma that has arisen but not ceased is called the "present life"; any dharma that has not arisen and not come to be is called the "future life."
[And only the present moment]
The scripture says:
"In the seen only the seen, in the heard only the heard, in the known only the known, in the perceived only the perceived."
and no wandering thoughts about past or future. In truth, people's mental unease, anxiety, and suffering are all born of wandering thoughts about the past or the future.
To be aware without thought or mental activity is called presence.

It was said earlier that whenever there is awareness there are no drifting thoughts; the "no thought, no mental activity" spoken of here means not only that there are no drifting thoughts, but that one does not actively give rise to thoughts either.
One should maintain the state of presence at all times and in all places. The Treasury of Buddhas Sutra says:
"The anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi of all Buddhas is entirely no-thought and no-mental-activity."
The Treatise on the Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna says:
"What is meant by awareness is that the essence of the mind is free from thought."
(Awareness means that the essence of the mind is free from thought.) The Essentials of the Transmission of the Mind says:
"Just as it is, it is; stir a thought and you miss it." "Still the thoughts and forget the reckonings, and the Buddha appears of himself."
Chan Master Da'an says:
"If you
(you all)
wish to become Buddhas, then
(you need only)

be without such a mass of inverted and clinging thoughts, wandering thoughts and evil notions, and defiled desires and impure minds of living beings — then you are Buddhas of initial resolve and true awakening."
(The Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp)

You can train your capacity for "seeing is just seeing" by being aware of a flower, a tree, a bottle, a chair, and so on; and train your capacity for "hearing is just hearing" by listening to music, to conversation around you, to the sound of traffic in the street, to the noise of machinery and equipment, and so on. Practice often. Do it long enough, and you will come to know the wonder of "focus the mind on one point, and there is nothing that cannot be done."

You may also be aware of the body or of a part of the body, for example a finger, a toe, the palm of the hand, the knee, an arm, a shoulder, and so on. Further still, you may be aware of your own nature, and aware of the present moment. All of these are being aware of the present moment and so abiding in presence. The preceding three chapters (awareness of movements, awareness of feelings, awareness of the breath), and the next chapter (awareness of thoughts), are likewise awareness of the present moment and therefore presence.
Feeling the body from within will also bring you into presence.
In daily life, form the habit of doing everything consciously. Never do anything unconsciously!

An example was given earlier, and it is repeated here because it is so very important. It is said that a fly came and settled on the Buddha's face, and the Buddha gently brushed it away with his hand. Then he made the gesture of brushing a second time. The disciples asked in wonder: "World-Honored One, the first time you waved your hand was to drive away the fly; what was the second wave for?" The Buddha answered: "The first was an unconscious movement, done without awareness, so I made the movement a second time with awareness, to correct it." In this manifestation the Buddha was teaching his disciples that every movement should be made consciously, with clear and distinct awareness, and that an unconscious movement is ignorance and must be corrected at once.

Whenever a wandering thought arises, at once turn your attention to awareness of the present moment and be present. In that moment, attend only to whether you are present, and pay no attention to what the wandering thought is doing. In this way you can dismantle and dissolve the wandering thought. (How easy or hard this is depends on how shallow or deep your practice of presence is. Only persevere, and its wonder cannot be spoken.) Conversely, if you resent the wandering thought and want to drive it out and destroy it, you are placing your attention on the wandering thought, which only makes it firmer and more ablaze.

A wandering thought is an alarm bell: when it rings, at once rouse your awareness and return to the present moment — be present, and stay present. A wandering thought is also a training partner: whenever it comes, dismantle it and dissolve it with presence. That is how the power of presence is raised.

Q: I have found presence to be a very easy and effective method of practice; it has solved quite a few practical problems for me, including mental unease, anxiety, and suffering. I hope you will explain presence in more detail.
A:
Stones from other hills may polish jade. To better understand presence, experience it, and apply it, you may read and watch:
Practicing the Power of Now
Stillness Speaks
How to Live Stress-Free (video)
and
The Astonishing Power of Yes (video)

. As you read and watch, note one point: their author (Eckhart Tolle) holds that "consciousness" is the one omnipresent essence of the universe and its supreme ruler, and that the self is a part or an embodiment of consciousness. This differs from the Buddhadharma, and that is why they are called "other hills."
Q: How does one become aware of one's own nature?

A: One's own nature is the inner spiritual energy. To be aware of the own-nature is to feel it, to become one with it, and to abide in it. For living beings, the body is the shell and the dwelling of the own-nature. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
"The physical body is a dwelling." Patriarch Linji says: "Just look at the puppets playing on the stage — all their pulling and tugging depends on the one within."
This says that the physical body is like a wooden puppet, and that what manipulates this physical body is the own-nature. Hence the Formula for Cultivating the Mind says:
"The hundred bones crumble and scatter, returning to fire and wind; one thing stays ever numinous, covering heaven and earth."

Throughout the twelve hours of the day, knowing hunger and knowing thirst, knowing cold and knowing heat, being angry or being glad — this is the own-nature. The physical body is a coming-together of the four conditions of earth, water, fire, and wind; its substance is inert and insentient — how could it see, hear, feel, and know? What can see, hear, feel, and know must be your own-nature. The patriarch says:

"The four elements do not understand speaking the Dharma or hearing the Dharma; empty space does not understand speaking the Dharma or hearing the Dharma. Only that which is before you now — clear and distinct, singly bright, without shape or form — understands speaking the Dharma and hearing the Dharma. That which is without shape or form is your own-nature."
The Laṅkāvatāra Sutra of the Mahāyāna says:
"Just as a wooden man or a raised corpse
(making a corpse rise and walk and move about)
, by the power of the piśāca's mechanism, shakes, moves, turns, and acts
(does)
without cease."

This says that the physical body, like a wooden man or a corpse, moves by the power of a mechanism. This mechanism-power is the life force of the own-nature. To be aware of the own-nature is to feel this living vitality within the body, and to become one with it and abide in it. If you maintain awareness of the own-nature, drifting thoughts do not arise, and you can easily and naturally attain no-thought, or single-thought. To be aware of the own-nature densely and without interruption is, at all times and in all places, to be aware of and to feel the living vitality of the own-nature within the body, and to become one with it and abide in it. In daily life, when conditions come, act; when conditions go, be still. Whether working or talking, maintain awareness of the own-nature, free and self-governing (not falling into wandering thoughts, not manipulated by conditions). The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
"Not departing from the own-nature — that is the field of merit."
Q: How does one become aware of the present moment?

A: To be aware of the present moment is to be deeply conscious of the present moment. When you are deeply conscious of the present moment, you are in a collected state in which you think neither of the past nor of the future. Of course, you may also be aware of the present moment itself — the space that holds the arising of all things. When you are aware of this space, you are likewise in a collected state in which you think neither of the past nor of the future.
Interviewed while sitting on a park bench, Eckhart Tolle said something quite illuminating: "When you sit here, just watch what is happening around you,
without any interpretation, simply being with the present moment exactly as it is

. In this way you will probably know what it is like to sit on a park bench. This moment, needing nothing added to it — sounds, sights, people, the sound of water, light and shadow — allow it to be exactly as it is. And that brings peace; you need not be forever caught up in events, thoughts, emotions, and reactions. You are the wider space in which all these things happen. You are the awareness behind all these things; without that awareness, none of this would be here, and in space there would be only atoms and molecules. You are the awareness that allows the whole world to exist; the awareness that can understand — that is the real you. Not by thinking concepts, but through actual realization. Step back and allow the phenomenal world to be just as it is now; allow this moment to be exactly as it is. This will take you deeper into yourself, and then you may discover a sudden peace in the background — it simply happens. Yet you must be alert; you need to stay alert, alert to the present moment as it is, alert to your senses, to your sensations, and to the energy behind those feelings — that is, awareness. Be alert. Without alertness, you drift into thinking and begin thinking about the next thing: What will happen to me tomorrow? There is a place for making plans, but it is not on a park bench. This is not the place to think about how tomorrow should be, because you will miss all the beauty and vitality around you (laughs). Then you feel cold, but you do not even need to think that what you feel is 'cold.' Right — it is only a sensation; you need not call it 'cold.' Even that is fine, it does not matter; in life there are no more conditioned reactions — always resisting, always opposing something, always wanting to grasp at something." (
Eckhart Tolle: Enlightenment in the Present Moment (video)
Q: How does one practice the skill of "mirroring things as a mirror does"?
A: Be aware of the present object without thought or mental activity. Master Yinguang says:

"If you wish the true knowing to appear, then in your daily words and deeds always rouse awareness and illumination, and do not let any unreasonable thoughts and feelings sprout in the mind even for a moment. Keep the mind always empty, bright, and penetrating. Like a mirror set on its stand, it reflects whatever appears; it only reflects the object before it and does not turn with it. Beauty and ugliness belong to the other — what has that to do with me? Do not plan for what comes, do not linger over what goes. If ever unreasonable thoughts and feelings stir even slightly, deal with them sternly and wipe them out completely."
(From the Preface to Liaofan's Four Lessons; for annotation see in detail
Annotated Liaofan's Four Lessons: Summary of the Original Preface
Q: When I am present, may I keep my mind on the dantian and cultivate both nature and life?

A: Yes. If while present you keep your mind on the jiaji, the effect will be even better. The jiaji, also called the jiaji double pass, is the xinshu acupoint. For the benefits of keeping the mind on the jiaji, see in detail
Reversing Aging by Cultivating the Jiaji
Xinshu
(shù)
acupoint
] Located one and a half cun to either side of the seventh thoracic vertebra (as in the figure below), it is the gate through which the heart's qi enters and exits

And since the heart governs the spirit and is the great ruler of the five viscera and six bowels, the jiaji acupoint is connected with the five viscera and six bowels; clearly the jiaji acupoint is no ordinary point
Draw the spirit inward.
Form the habit of looking within.
Hold fast to each present moment of the mind.

To be aware of thoughts is to know one's own mind. The mind here means the thoughts that arise when the six sense faculties come into contact with the six sense objects. A practitioner must at all times know his own thoughts — in raising troops to put down bandits, one must know where the bandits are. And the importance of contemplating the mind goes far beyond this.

Patriarch Bodhidharma's Treatise on Breaking the Marks says: "The single Dharma of contemplating the mind encompasses all dharmas; it is the most essential and direct." The Sutra of the Mahāyāna Contemplation of the Mind-Ground says: "Within the three realms, the mind is sovereign. One who can contemplate the mind attains ultimate liberation; one who cannot remains forever in bondage." It also says: "This method (contemplating the mind) is called the supreme secret mind-ground Dharma-gate of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions; this method is called the Dharma-gate of sudden awakening by which all ordinary beings enter the Tathāgata's ground; this method is called the true straight path by which all bodhisattvas proceed to great bodhi; this method is called the subtle jewel-palace in which the Buddhas of the three periods enjoy the Dharma-bliss themselves; this method is called the inexhaustible treasury of benefit for all sentient beings." It also says: "If one can cultivate this profound and wonderful contemplation, the fruit of delusion, karma, and suffering has no way to arise; contemplate only the true suchness of ultimate reality, and both subject and object are forgotten, beyond all views." The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: "All Tathāgatas, from the very ground of their initial resolve, rely upon the perfect illumination of the pure awareness-mark, forever cutting off ignorance, and only then accomplish the Buddha path." The Nirvāṇa Sutra says: "To be able to contemplate the nature of the mind is called supreme samādhi."

Master Taixu says in his Lectures on the Sutra of the Mahāyāna Contemplation of the Mind-Ground: "(This sutra) points out the awakening of the intentions of Mahāyāna practitioners; it is a most reliable and practical Dharma-gate." "Although this sutra runs to as many as thirteen chapters, the 'Chapter on Contemplating the Mind' is especially important. If a practitioner can contemplate the mind and know the mind to be illusory and still, he will not be deluded and clinging; when clinging is gone, deluded confusion can no longer arise; when confusion does not arise, wisdom grows; as wisdom grows, afflictions are extinguished — confusion extinguished and wisdom born. This is of practical use to the practitioner, and he accomplishes the virtue of cutting off."

[The six sense faculties] Eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. [The six sense objects] Objects of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects. "Dust" means defilement: they can defile people's pure minds and prevent the true nature from manifesting. The six sense objects are also called the six domains, that is, the domains taken as objects by the six sense faculties. [The virtue of cutting off] All afflictions cut off, pure and unconditioned, liberated and free. This is one of the Buddha's three virtues. The Buddha's three virtues are: the virtue of wisdom, the virtue of grace, and the virtue of cutting off.

Awareness of thoughts has three links: first, seeking the strayed mind; second, knowing without following; third, not departing from the present thought. Among these, "knowing without following" is the central link that carries on what comes before and opens what follows.
To be aware of the present moment is called the mind being present — this is awareness; to fall into wandering thoughts is for the mind to be absent — this is delusion. Mencius says:

"When a man's chickens and dogs stray, he knows to go after them; but when his mind strays, he does not know to go after it. The way of learning is nothing else: it is simply seeking the strayed mind."
(Mencius

Book of Gaozi) (Translation: Some people, when their chickens and dogs are lost, know enough to go and fetch them back; when their mind is lost, they do not know enough to go and fetch it back. The learning of how to be a person is nothing else — it is simply fetching back that lost mind.)
[The way of learning] The "learning" here does not mean systematic knowledge, but the cultivation of mind and nature, the learning of how to be a person.

The mind being present means the mind is aware of the present moment. Draw back the mind that has fallen into the world of the head (wandering thoughts) and be aware of the present moment (this time, this place, this matter) — living in the present moment: this is the first step in awareness of thoughts. The ordinary person's mind is like a wild horse, a mad elephant, a cunning ape; it cannot be controlled in the least and is always in wandering thoughts. Drawing the mind back is escaping from the world of the head (wandering thoughts) — an extremely important step; as it is said, "focus the mind on one point, and there is nothing that cannot be done." Conversely, if the mind is scattered, nothing can be accomplished. Cultivation is the cultivation of the mind; if the mind is scattered, all the practice one does is empty, like what the martial world calls fancy posturing.

Therefore you must take charge of your own thoughts. Look after your thoughts at all times and in all places; if they stray, at once draw them back and keep them in the present moment. Keep practicing the gathering of the mind: lose it and recover it at once. There are many ways to gather the mind; by trying them out you can find the one that suits you best.

Here is one method: ask yourself in self-reflection, "Master, is the mind present?" At once turn the light around and see whether your mind has strayed. When you look carefully, the mind is drawn back, and you answer yourself: "Present." This is a cultivation full of interest. Do it often, and when your practice is deep the mind will settle; even if it strays, a single keen wakefulness brings it back.

Huike (later the Second Patriarch of Chan) came to Patriarch Bodhidharma and said: "My mind is not at peace; I beg the Master to set my mind at peace." Bodhidharma said: "Bring me your mind, and I will set it at peace for you." Huike said: "Seeking the mind, it is utterly unobtainable." Bodhidharma said: "I have finished setting your mind at peace for you."

This is the wonderful method of setting the mind at peace transmitted by Patriarch Bodhidharma: seeking the mind. When thoughts disturb you, look carefully at the thought and see what it actually wants to think; the thought then naturally subsides and the mind settles — as it is said, "observe the thought and the thought settles (stops)." (This wonderful method of setting the mind at peace is extremely effective. If you cannot yet get a grip on it, or find it very taxing, it means that your awareness is not yet strong enough; you may set it aside for the time being and do it later, when your awareness is strong.)
Through constant practice, once you have a preliminary foundation in gathering the mind, you need only remind yourself — "The present moment!" — and the mind is drawn back.

Often observe: is the mind present, or has it strayed? If the mind is in the present moment — that is, on this time, this place, or this matter (what is being done right now) — then it is present. If the mind is wandering, thinking of another time, another place, or another matter, then it has strayed and must at once be drawn back, so that "dressing is just dressing, eating is just eating," aware of the present moment.
Single-minded in the thought that a swan is about to arrive" — this is the classic case of wandering thoughts. The Mencius

Book of Gaozi, Part One says: "Yi Qiu was the finest player in the whole state. Suppose Yi Qiu were to teach two men to play chess: one of them concentrates with single-minded devotion, listening only to Yi Qiu; the other, though he listens, is all the while thinking that a swan is about to come, and wants to bend his bow and shoot it. Though he learns together with the other, he does not equal him. Is it that his intelligence is inferior? I say: no, it is not so." (Translation: Yi Qiu was the finest chess player in the whole state. Suppose Yi Qiu taught two men to play chess: one of them concentrated with single-minded devotion, listening only to Yi Qiu's teaching and thinking of nothing else; the other, though he was listening, kept thinking that a swan was about to fly over, and wanted to take up a bow and arrow to shoot it. Thus, although the same teacher taught them, he learned less well than the first. Can one say that his intelligence was inferior to the other's? I say: it was not so.)

Originally, our thinking exists to serve our survival in this world of forms. Thinking should therefore be like tap water: turn it on when needed, turn it off when not. It should also be like a servant, wholly obedient to the sovereign, never acting on its own. But the present situation is exactly the opposite: thinking is domineering and wilful, it controls you, and it is forever turned on and never off, daydreaming without end and sending wandering thoughts flying. Cultivation means the master regains authority and makes thinking obey you. In the Sutra of the Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching, the Buddha says: "The mind is more to be feared than a venomous snake, a savage beast, or a vengeful thief; a raging fire sweeping all before it is no adequate simile. Suppose a man holds a vessel of honey and walks along carelessly, seeing only the honey and not the deep pit. Suppose a mad elephant without a hook, or a monkey that has gained a tree, leaping and jumping beyond all restraint. You must promptly beat it down and not let it run wild. Let this mind loose, and a person's good works are ruined; focus it on one point, and there is nothing that cannot be done. Therefore, monks, be diligent and subdue your minds."

The mind being present means the mind is on this time, this place, or this matter (what is being done now), without clinging or wandering thoughts. There are two situations of "the mind being present": one is the mind in a state of working, the other is the mind in a state of stillness. When life or business requires the mind to work, the mind is in the working state, and then one should think with single-minded devotion; when the mind is not needed for work, it should be in the state of stillness, without thought or mental activity, and must never drift into endless imagining. So the practice of the mind being present should be done from these two sides.

Then how can the mind be single-mindedly devoted when it works? And how can it be without thought when it is still? Since this book is entirely concerned with cultivation, the emphasis is on how the mind can be without thought or mental activity. The Treasury of Buddhas Sutra says: "The anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi of all dharmas is entirely no-thought and no-mental-activity." The Essentials of the Transmission of the Mind says: "Still the thoughts and forget the reckonings, and the Buddha appears of himself." As for how to achieve the single-minded presence of the mind when reciting the Buddha's name, contemplating the mind, or practicing Chan, the relevant chapters discuss this in detail.

There are many methods for making the mind without thought or mental activity; here we focus on the method of awareness of the present moment. When you are focused in your awareness of the present moment (deeply conscious of the present moment), the mind is in a state of no-thought and no-mental-activity. For drifting thoughts are all about thinking back and forth, having nothing to do with the present moment, and their aim is to drag you away from it. So in this section you should work hard specifically at awareness of the present moment (the mind being present). Be aware of the present moment without a break between thoughts, until movement and stillness become one piece, keeping the spirit terrace clear and bright. "Clear" means no-thought; "bright" means awareness.
[The spirit terrace] Refers to the mind, the heart.

The past is already past, the future has not yet come; all you can possess is this present moment, and the quality of this moment genuinely affects your future. So to place all your attention on this present moment — the mind being present — is of the utmost importance. This is why the Chan patriarchs always taught people to live in the present moment.

To cultivate focused, continuous, and lasting awareness is of the greatest importance. In the practice of the mind being present, be present with focus, be present continuously, be present lastingly. In a word: be present with focus, continuity, and endurance!
Q: I am focused in my awareness of the present moment, and yet wandering thoughts keep coming. What should I do?

A: This shows that your awareness is not yet strong enough. You should strengthen the earlier stages of practice — awareness of movements, awareness of feelings, and awareness of the breath — and lay the foundation solid before beginning the practice of "awareness of thoughts."

What is called "the mind being present" is the mind focused on what is seen, heard, or done, with no other thought. This is the key to "dressing and eating are also cultivation." Grasp this key, and you can cultivate at all times and in all places. In this way you not only have ample time for cultivation, so that work and cultivation do not interfere with each other, but your practice is uninterrupted and accomplishment comes easily.

When your practice is deep, you will find that "the mind being present" is most wonderful and full of delight; this is the state of Chan. Check at all times: is the mind present? The moment you check, the mind settles. Practice in your leisure, practice while working, practice while waiting, practice in the midst of irritation and unease.

A student asked Chan Master Zhaozhou: What should one who has understood the mind and seen the nature be like? Master Zhaozhou replied: He should practice greatly. The student said: I wonder whether a master of your attainment still practices? Master Zhaozhou said: I just dress and eat. The student said: Dressing and eating are ordinary matters — can these really be cultivation? Master Zhaozhou said: If they were not cultivation, then tell me, what do I do every day? (Original text: "Question: What is one who has finished the matter like? The Master said: He is practicing greatly. The student said: I wonder whether the Master still practices or not? The Master said: Dressing and eating. The student said: Dressing and eating are ordinary matters; I wonder whether this is cultivation or not? The Master said: You tell me, what do I do every day?" (Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhaozhou))

Master Hanshan says: "Someone asked: 'The ancients, when hungry, ate; when tired, slept — and that was the Way. People today, when hungry, eat; when tired, sleep — why is that not the Way?' The answer: 'The ancients, eating, only ate; sleeping, only slept — and so it was the Way. People today, eating, do not eat; sleeping, do not sleep, but (instead) give themselves to wild and random calculations — and so they turn their backs on the Way.' From this we see that in your daily life you need only lift your eyebrows and give a shout — enough to startle the spirits and frighten the ghosts, to shatter the courage of heavenly demons and scatter the souls of yin ghosts — one shout drives them off, and you are left in the original ground, still and silent, not a thread hanging, bare and stark, utterly naked. Take up this one family style: when you would read, then read; when you do not read, set it aside and do not hang a single word there. When you would write, then write; when you do not write, set it aside and do not indulge in random calculations. Even in drinking tea and eating food, just drink tea and eat food; when you would sleep, then sleep; when you must relieve yourself, then relieve yourself. Whatever you meet, be done with it, and do not allow any reckoning afterwards. Be like a wandering ghost, clean and pure, spotless and white — yet you must not sit down inside that cleanliness and purity (do not lose your awareness and fall into blankness). In this way, going straight in with a single blade, with one thought pressing forward, when you read you see the ancients face to face, and when you write it is only a single mouthful spat out from your own breast, with no before or after. The time of storing up is the time of pouring out, and the time of pouring out is the time of storing up. In this way you are not turned about by movement and stillness, by light and dark, nor moved by any manner of trickery." (Dream Roaming Collection, "Instruction to Huang Weiheng")
Q: When I practice gathering the mind, I draw it back but cannot keep it; it runs off again at once, and I watch it go with my eyes wide open, helpless. What should I do?

A: When the mind has been drawn back, you must tether it with awareness — this is usually called keeping the mind. For example, do one thing with single-minded devotion (especially the trivial chores of daily life, which are the best objects of practice), with the mind undistracted and perfectly clear; or be aware of movements, be aware of the breath; or be aware of a flower, a tree, an object without giving rise to thoughts — mirroring things as a mirror does, tying the mind to one point. So the key to keeping the mind is: aware, yet without giving rise to thoughts. The practices of gathering the mind and keeping the mind rest on the earlier cultivation of awareness. If, when gathering the mind, you find that your awareness is not strong enough and you cannot draw it back (you fall into the world of wandering thoughts and cannot extricate yourself), or you draw it back but cannot keep it, then you must strengthen the earlier three stages (awareness of movements, awareness of feelings, and awareness of the breath).
Q: Wandering thoughts often fly up when I am lying in bed. What should I do?

A: If ever this happens, at once be aware of the breath, or be aware of movements, or of feelings — you may, for instance, rub your fingers. The method of rubbing the fingers is: with the thumb slowly and repeatedly rub (stroke) the middle finger and the index finger, being focusedly aware of each movement and of the sensation of contact between the fingers, the mind following the fingers. When you are familiar with this practice, body and mind enter easily into a state that is serene and still, and yet aware. Whenever and wherever you keep on indulging in wandering thoughts, that is a wretched business: it is delusion, it is dreaming the dream of saṃsāra. At such a time you must at once rouse a keen wakefulness, draw the mind back, and focus on what you are doing; or be aware of the breath, or of movements, or of feelings; or be aware of the present moment: dwell in the present moment together with everything around you without giving rise to thoughts, so that objects do not disturb the mind and the mind does not chase objects. Do this often, and you will grope your way to a whole set of methods that keep you in the state of awareness, abiding in the present moment.

The method of being aware of thoughts is: observe your own thoughts without judgment. This point of "without judgment" is very important, otherwise you add delusion upon delusion. The key is: knowing without following.
The Treatise on Generating the Bodhi Mind says:
"If a deluded mind arises
(if a wandering thought arises)
, know it and do not follow it; when the delusion subsides
(when the wandering thought subsides)
, the mind-source is empty and still, the ten thousand virtues are all complete, and its wondrous function is inexhaustible."
[Knowing without following] Watch the thought without judgment: in the thought, no thought.

[Mind-source] The mind is the source of all dharmas, hence "mind-source." [The ten thousand virtues are all complete] The ten thousand virtues are complete. "Si" means "then, indeed." Example: with preparation, one can then be free of calamity.

When you are aware of thoughts and observe your thinking, you experience the existence of the master — it is the master who is aware of thoughts and observes thinking. This master is you, and thoughts are not you. When a thought arises and you run after it, it controls you, and you may even take it to be yourself. If a thought arises and you do not run after it but know it without following, then you are the master. This is freedom — to exist autonomously. Since beginningless kalpas, living beings have been deluded and inverted precisely because they run after thoughts, giving rise to confusion and creating karma, so that birth and death and saṃsāra continue without end. Now, to end birth and death and leave saṃsāra, the urgent task is to escape the control of the head and become one who is free.

The key to contemplating the mind is: look at the present thought. When a wandering thought arises, look at it carefully and it disappears; after a while it arises again, and looking carefully again, it disappears once more; if no wandering thought arises, simply watch. Continue in this way, and when it has long been pure and familiar, and you see not a single thought arise, you are then in accord with prajñā. At this time there is contemplation without thought, and no-thought yet contemplating. The Awakening of Faith says: "If there is one who can contemplate no-thought, he is thereby tending toward the Buddha's wisdom." The state of no-thought is excellent, and deep, vast, and endless — but do not pursue or cling to it. When thoughts are present, know them and do not follow them; when thoughts are absent, still maintain awareness — still and yet illuminating, illuminating and yet still. As it is said, "with thoughts, contemplate the thought; without thoughts, contemplate emptiness." Look to where a thought arises; if a thought arises, you must see it at once. If you practice contemplation of the mind ever more deeply, subduing afflictions, removing habitual tendencies, leaving sorrow and suffering behind, and attaining one mind undisturbed — all this comes naturally. Patriarch Bodhidharma says: "The single Dharma of contemplating the mind encompasses all dharmas; it is the most essential and direct." (Treatise on Breaking the Marks)

If your practice of looking at the present thought has matured, then when contemplating the mind, turn the light around: look at what the next thought is (in the original, "what is the next thought?"). Or: is a thought arising or not? This too is a very effective method of stilling delusion.

You should often observe (be aware of) your thoughts; this is very beneficial and very interesting. Generally speaking, there are three situations. First, the observation is focused and continuous, and at that time there is only right mindfulness (the thought of awareness) and no wandering thoughts. Second, the observation is not continuous, so right mindfulness and wandering thoughts alternate. In that case, carefully observe the logical relationship between the preceding thought and the following thought; this is not only interesting but also helps you understand this so-called "self" better, and helps you pass over into the first situation. Third, observation is lost and you fall entirely into wandering thoughts, so that there are only wandering thoughts and no right mindfulness. The first situation is what we want to attain; the second must be carried on under supervision; the third must be completely eliminated.

Awareness of thoughts is a sharp weapon for stilling delusion, removing clinging, and breaking through confusion; the ancients likened it to a demon-revealing mirror. Likewise, this practice should be done not only while sitting but also a great deal off the cushion: practice while walking, standing, sitting, and lying down; practice with the eyes open and with them closed; practice at every available moment — practice! practice! practice! Form the habit of contemplating the mind at all times and in all places, until habit becomes second nature.
Q: When I contemplate the mind, I cannot see any thoughts. What should I do?

A: At the beginning this happens; there is no need to fret — just know that you are focused in contemplating the mind, and that is enough. If your attention is lost, at once draw it back: lose it and recover it at once. Be sure to cultivate the capacity and habit of focused, continuous, and lasting contemplation of the mind. Further, you must accomplish this: if a wandering thought arises, know it and do not follow it.
Q: When I contemplate the mind, my head easily becomes dizzy. What should I do?

A: On this point, Mr. Nan Huaijin says: "The pure prajñā method of contemplating the mind observes the arising and ceasing of one's own mind, intellect, and consciousness; there is originally no question of where to begin contemplating — to fuss so is to make unnecessary trouble! The mind is not inside, outside, or in between. Yet when ordinary practitioners do this contemplation, they easily concentrate attention in the head, bringing on high blood pressure and other ailments; hence the further provision of the expedient of contemplating gently at the heart. And lest you not understand the region of the heart, it is specifically explained as being here at the pit of the chest, between the two nipples, at the hollow where the ribs meet (
usually called the yellow court, the heart wheel, or the heart, and also the location of the Shanzhong acupoint
). It is right here that contemplation naturally arises." (A Beginner's Course in Samādhi and Prajñā)
Q: Sometimes a wandering thought circles and will not leave. What should I do?

A: Just quiet your mind and observe that thinker closely, observe it without any judgment, and see what it wants to think. When you observe in this way, the power of the wandering thought weakens sharply and it will finally subside. If it arises again after a while, observe it in the same way until it subsides. This is "observe the thought and the thought settles (stops)"; it is a good method for stopping wandering thoughts. Once you have got the knack of gathering the mind and observing delusion, some creative methods will surface of themselves; then take up the ever-deepening cycle of "practice, summarize, improve (draw up a new plan); practice again, summarize again, improve again (draw up a new plan)." In time you will form a whole set of all-weather methods of your own.

Always observe with curiosity and keen interest what that thinker is thinking, and accomplish knowing without following. In this way you are both stilling delusion and cultivating awareness — two gains in one. Throughout the whole course of studying and practicing awareness while reciting the Buddha's name, focused, continuous, and lasting awareness is extremely important; when awareness is strong, everything is easy. So seize every time and every opportunity to strengthen awareness as much as you can; this is the most basic and most effective method.
Q: Who is it that observes that thinker?
